ai-b15a6fb967.headline: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks”
ai-b15a6fb967.fulltext:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.
The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.
“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post.
OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.
The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.
Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”
“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”
The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.
Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.
To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”
Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.

ai-e6978f097e.headline: ‘Black October’: cybersecurity experts sound the alarm over new era of AI-enabled hacking
ai-e6978f097e.fulltext:
Leaders in cybersecurity are sounding the alarm after the discovery of a major vulnerability this week. They are predicting that artificial intelligence tools will expose more fundamental weaknesses in global internet infrastructure in the months to come.
“I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” said Sam Altman on Thursday evening, joining the chorus of executives. In the midst of what’s being called “Black October”, for which researchers used AI to help identify critical flaws in a coding language that is used across millions of websites and may have been unpatched for years, tech executives are warning about the ways AI will be used both to identify and exploit security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented scale and pace.
The next few months will see a “vulnerability tsunami”, according to Jason Clinton, Anthropic’s deputy chief information security officer. “There won’t be enough time to patch critical infrastructure,” Clinton said in a post on X on Thursday evening. Marc Benioff, the Salesforce CEO, agreed and called it a “code red”.
AI is uniquely able to find and identify security flaws in a way and at a pace that will feel catastrophic because the security community will not be able to move quickly enough to address them, said Matthew Prince, the Cloudflare CEO. “It’s going to feel like the sky is falling. It’s going to feel like there’s nothing we can do.
“The next two years are going to be incredibly, incredibly, incredibly fraught with new tools that have infinite patience to go look for vulnerabilities across the Internet,” he wrote in a post on X.
While cybersecurity experts have been warning about a “vulnpocalypse”, or the ability for AI to more easily identify security bugs for months, it wasn’t until “Black October” that researchers were able to use AI to find a flaw as fundamental and critical as the one announced on 21 October.
Massive bugs were found in a programming language called PHP, which may have left the millions of websites that run on it vulnerable to hackers for years. Some experts estimated 70% of all the sites on the internet were at risk of hacking.
However, in the same way AI will be used to aid in identifying security vulnerabilities at an unprecedented pace, tech leaders worry it’ll also be used by malicious actors to exploit those bugs at an unprecedented pace.
Attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability have already begun.
After the vulnerabilities were announced, government and private websites across the US and UK temporarily took down their sites to patch the bugs. The US National Security Agency (NSA) issued an alert recommending any site that runs on PHP implement the patches immediately. Malicious cyberactors may seek to further exploit these bugs to access servers without authorization, the NSA said.
“Such an access vector could help attackers steal sensitive data, disrupt services or move deeper into a network,” the warning read.
In a post on X, Prince said CloudFlare, a security provider, had seen evidence of thousands of people trying to exploit the PHP flaws in the 10 hours before it was announced.
“That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now,” he wrote.
In a blogpost, researchers at AI security platform Wiz said that this was “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history”.
“The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” they wrote.

work-careers-c6ad88f7fd.headline: AI slows hiring at India’s GCCs as headcount per center stalls
work-careers-c6ad88f7fd.fulltext:
AI slows hiring at India’s GCCs as headcount per center stalls
- India had 2,117 GCCs after 400+ opened in the two years to March 2026.
- GCC headcount rose 24% to more than 2.36 million, per Zinnov.
- Workers per GCC are roughly 1,115 this year, down from 1,130 in 2024.
- Zinnov puts 55% of GCC work under AI displacement pressure.
BENGALURU, INDIA — Multinationals’ global capability centers (GCCs) in India, a major source of tech jobs as domestic software firms cut back, are turning cautious on hiring as artificial intelligence (AI) pushes companies to rethink large workforces. The number of centers keeps rising, but the average team at each one has stopped growing.
More centers, flatter teams
More than 400 GCCs were set up in India in the two years to March 2026, taking the total to 2,117, according to Zinnov estimates cited by Nikkei Asia. Employee count rose 24% to more than 2.36 million.
Workers per GCC grew to 1,130 in 2024 from about 910 in 2019, but the figure is roughly 1,115 this year. Visa, Technicolour, PayPal and Fidelity have each cut hundreds of positions at their Indian centers.
“Our whole industry was based on how many people we could hire because work output was directly proportional to the number of people,” said Lalit Ahuja, chief executive at ANSR, which helps companies build GCCs. He said “the newer GCCs and even the incumbents are rationalizing headcount.”
Work in AI’s path
Zinnov classifies nearly 18% of GCC work as commodity tasks such as software testing and 37% as procedural work such as software development, implying 55% of GCC portfolios are under displacement pressure. Praveen Bhadada, chief executive at consultancy Neovay, estimates about 25 GCCs in India closed or were sold in the fiscal year that ended in March, a number he expects to double this year.
Some centers are changing hands. Tata Consultancy Services recently took over American retailer Best Buy’s India GCC, following HCLTech‘s acquisition of Guardian Life’s GCC in August. Bhadada said AI could “seriously come after commodity jobs that are in India.”
Rivals, and a bet on new entrants
India hosts nearly 40% of the world’s GCCs, according to UnearthIQ, but Poland, Hungary, Romania, Brazil and Mexico are competing for the work. European sites help with General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) compliance, while Mexico and Costa Rica share business hours with the United States.
UnearthIQ chief executive Gaurav Vasu said struggling GCCs are more likely to transform than close. “The future will be led by small and midsize GCCs built around AI-native applications,” he said.
Ahuja expects new entrants such as McDonald’s and Starbucks, and expansions by Sanofi and JP Morgan, to help offset the reduction in headcount.
For companies running or planning a global capability center (GCC) in India, the data point to smaller, AI-skilled teams rather than headcount growth. Firms comparing a captive center with a provider-run global delivery center can start with the top AI outsourcing companies list.

On the NSE, the stock closed at ₹1,133.80, a 61.97% premium to its issue price and 2.26% below its listing price of ₹1,160. During the session, shares touched highs of ₹1,209.85 on the BSE and ₹1,211 on the NSE, representing gains of 72.84% and 73%, respectively, over the issue price. At the BSE closing price, Tonbo Imaging’s market capitalisation stood at ₹6,493.79 Cr ($684.1 Mn). Original | October 23, 2026, 10:00 IST Defence tech company Tonbo Imaging made a strong stock market debut, listing at ₹1,162 on the BSE, a 66% premium to its issue price of ₹700 per share. On the NSE, the stock debuted at ₹1,160, translating into a listing gain of 65.71%. The company commanded a market capitalisation of ₹6,656.18 Cr (about $701.3 Mn) on the BSE at its listing price. The debut followed strong investor demand for Tonbo’s ₹852 Cr IPO, which was open for subscription from October 15 to October 19 at a price band of ₹665-₹700 per share. The public issue was subscribed 135.9X, attracting bids for 115.87 Cr shares against the 85.26 Lakh shares on offer. The IPO comprised entirely an offer for sale (OFS) of around 1.22 Cr shares by existing shareholders, with no fresh issue component. Consequently, Tonbo will receive no proceeds from the public offering. Tonbo’s cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza collectively pocketed ₹137.2 Cr by selling shares through the IPO, with Lakshmikumar accounting for ₹80.5 Cr of the proceeds. Ahead of the bidding, the company secured ₹255.4 Cr from anchor investors, allotting 36.5 Lakh shares to 43 investors at ₹700 apiece. Participants included SBI Mutual Fund, Goldman Sachs, BlackRock, and WhiteOak Capital. Inside Tonbo’s Defence Business Tonbo was bought out from Sarnoff Corporation in 2012 by promoters and cofounders Arvind Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar, and Cecilia D’Souza. It subsequently pivoted from research and technology development services to designing advanced imaging and sensor systems for military applications. Its portfolio includes thermal imaging systems, weapon sights, fire-control systems, and missile seekers used for surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting. The startup handles prototype development, system integration, and qualification testing in-house, while outsourcing manufacturing to partners including Kaynes Technology and Avalon Technology. The strong listing comes despite a decline in Tonbo’s FY26 financial performance. Operating revenue fell 22.7% YoY to ₹362.6 Cr from ₹469.1 Cr, while net profit declined about 30% to ₹50.8 Cr from ₹72.8 Cr. In Q1 FY27, the startup reported a net loss of ₹17.7 Cr on operating revenue of ₹36 Cr. Speaking to Inc42, CEO Lakshmikumar attributed the FY26 revenue decline to delays in executing international programmes, which pushed deliveries into FY27.

Bank of India expects to gain nearly Rs 100 crore a quarter from UPI MDR
The proposed 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate (MDR) on eligible UPI merchant transactions above Rs 2,000 could open up a new revenue stream for banks, with Bank of India expecting to gain nearly Rs 100 crore from the framework. BoI had more than 11.01 lakh POS terminals and QR codes as of September 30, 2026, according to its investor presentation.
State owned Bank of India expects to gain nearly Rs 100 crore from the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) on select Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transactions on a quarterly basis, its Managing Director & CEO Rajneesh Karnatak told ETBFSI.
The estimate comes as the government introduces a fee framework for select high-value merchant transactions on UPI, creating a new revenue stream for banks and payment companies. Brokerages estimate that the move could generate an annual revenue pool of Rs 15,000-20,600 crore for the digital payments and banking ecosystem, although the eventual gains will depend on eligible transaction volumes and the role individual institutions play in the payment chain.
The bank had a network of more than 11.01 lakh point-of-sale (POS) terminals and QR codes as of September 30, 2026, according to the presentation. It has also launched a UPI-linked RuPay credit card under the PM SVANidhi scheme for street vendors and is developing its interoperable Banking Connect platform for merchant transactions.
Under the new framework, a 0.4 per cent MDR applies to specified person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, subject to a cap of Rs 300 per transaction. Certain categories attract concessional rates, while person-to-person payments and most merchant transactions remain outside the charge. The government has said around 96 per cent of merchant transactions will remain unaffected.
The MDR will be distributed across participants in the payments ecosystem. Under the reported sharing arrangement, 40 per cent of the fee goes to the customer’s issuing bank, 30 per cent to the merchant-acquiring bank, 20 per cent to the UPI application and 10 per cent to the bank supporting the application. The amount earned by an individual bank will therefore depend on its position in the payment chain and the transactions routed through it.
The proposed MDR marks a shift from the zero-MDR model that has governed most UPI payments since 2020.

global-economics-535c5bc037.headline: Infosys caps dull second quarter for Indian IT
global-economics-535c5bc037.fulltext:
Jas BardiaPublished23 Oct 2026, 09:58 PM IST
Infosys Ltd reported its slowest second-quarter performance in at least a decade on Friday, capping a modest quarterly outing for the country’s five largest tech services firms. The company's ADRs (American Depositary Receipts) tumbled on the New York Exchange, as India's second-largest information technology (IT) services firm dialled down its revenue guidance for the year.
Infosys ended the July-September period with $5.15 billion in revenue, marginally below a Bloomberg poll estimate of $5.18 billion. Three-fourths of the revenue growth—up 1.24% sequentially and 1.3% from a year earlier—came from energy, utilities and resources firms, which make up more than a tenth of its business.
With this, the country’s five largest tech services have clocked their slowest second quarter growth in three years. Tata Consultancy Services Ltd, HCL Technologies Ltd and Tech Mahindra Ltd ended the quarter with $7.64 billion, $3.72 billion, and $1.69 billion in revenue, up 0.24%, 2.03%, and 1.99% on a sequential basis, respectively. Wipro Ltd reported a decline in revenue at $2.61 billion, down 0.11% sequentially.
At least three of the Big Five, including TCS, HCL Tech and Wipro, have reported their worst second-quarter growth in three years. Much of this can be attributed to an uncertain demand environment marked by tensions in West Asia, which is forcing clients to pull back on non-essential tech spending. Rise in automation tools is also forcing companies to pass on savings to clients, pressuring revenue.
The management pointed to the challenging macroeconomic environment, hinting at rising competition and increasing client demand to save costs using artificial intelligence (AI).
“Now, the macro environment is also equally in a place where there are continuing different wars. There were some interest rate increases. There was also the 10-year yield, which is now neighbouring to 5%, and there's continuing some element of tariffs, which creates a different type of an environment for the global economy, and therefore for the type of clients that we work with, which is essentially the Global 2000,” said Salil Parekh, chief executive officer (CEO) of Infosys, during the company’s post-earnings press conference on Friday.
The Infosys commentary matches that of three of its peers. Earlier this month, TCS and Wipro’s management said the demand environment remains unchanged, adding that non-essential tech spending is under scrutiny, whereas HCL Tech’s management said the demand environment remains fluid as it is influenced by various factors. Tech Mahindra’s CEO was more optimistic, stating that the argument around deflationary headwinds was overblown.
Infosys lowered its full-year revenue growth guidance to 1-2% in constant currency terms, from 1.5-3% growth estimate outlined in the preceding quarter. This is its lowest full-year guidance issued in the second quarter in at least seven years. Constant currency does not take currency fluctuations into account. Investors took note, with the company's ADRs trading 5% lower at 8:15pm IST.
The muted results come ahead of a leadership change, with Ashiss Kumar Dash replacing CEO Parekh next April at the end of a nine-year tenure.
The company may just have to buy growth as its organic revenue may have declined.
“Assuming acquisition contribution remains at around 170 bps (basis points), the revised guidance implies an organic growth midpoint of around -0.2% versus 0.5-0.6% earlier. While Q2 performance was broadly in line with expectations, the guidance cut reflects weaker H2 visibility, continued pricing pressure and cautious client spending,” said Manav Medewala, research analyst at Mirae Asset Sharekhan.
Non-essential tech spending among retailers and high-tech companies during the period was lower than expected, said Jayesh Sanghrajka, chief financial officer, Infosys.
This also implies Noida-based HCLTech may grow faster than its Bengaluru peer this fiscal, as it expects revenue growth between 2.5-4% for the full year. To be sure, none of the other three companies share full-year revenue guidance.
Infosys’ first-half revenue rose 2.1% from the preceding year to $10.28 billion.
This comes as the company's profitability is under pressure. The company’s operating margins fell 10 basis points to 21% last quarter. Much of this was because of post-sales customer support. This makes Infosys the first of the Big Five to report a fall in margins last quarter.
TCS, HCLTech, Wipro, and Tech Mahindra reported 24%, 18.2%, 16.5%, and 14.8% in operating margins, respectively. While TCS’s margins remained unchanged from the preceding quarter, HCLTech, Wipro, and Tech Mahindra’s profitability rose 130 basis points, 50 basis points, and 40 basis points, respectively.
In terms of headcount, Infosys added headcount by 4,480 to 332,542 employees. Similar to last year, the company plans on hiring 20,000 freshers.
With this, the Big Five had a mixed result. Wipro cut headcount by more than 6,700 whereas TCS, HCLTech, and Tech Mahindra added more than 4,200 employees, 6,400 employees, and 5,400 employees, respectively.

global-economics-2af34a88de.headline: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’
global-economics-2af34a88de.fulltext:
The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

climate-energy-058610801d.headline: Chart: A record two-thirds of car sales in China are now electric vehicles
climate-energy-058610801d.fulltext:
Chart: A record two-thirds of car sales in China are now electric vehicles
For the first time, new-energy vehicles (NEVs) made up 67% of new car sales in China in September, according to the latest data from the China Passenger Car Association (CPCA).
The figures show that NEVs, which include battery electric cars and plug-in hybrids, captured a record share of sales, even though fewer were sold than last year.
This is because sales of combustion-engine cars are falling steeply, a trend that the CPCA has attributed to rising petrol prices following the start of the Hormuz crisis.
Indeed, sales of fuel-only cars were down 31% year-on-year in the first nine months of 2026, with plug-in hybrid sales down 26% – whereas battery EV sales were only down 4%.
One analyst tells Carbon Brief that China’s rapidly growing EV fleet has offset demand for 143m barrels of oil since the start of the Hormuz crisis.
Another says that the crisis is “reinforcing China’s electrification of road transport”.
Meanwhile, amid slowing domestic sales, Chinese carmakers’ exports of NEVs more than doubled [in 2026 to date / in September] from a year earlier.
NEV record
A record two out of every three cars sold in September in China were NEVs, according to CPCA data, as shown in the figure below.
(NEVs predominantly include battery electric vehicles – BEVs – and plug-in hybrids – PHEVs. BEVs only run on electricity, whereas PHEVs also have a combustion engine.)
This marks a rapid rise for NEVs from just 6% of new car sales in 2020 up to 58% in 2026 to date – and a record 67% in the month of September.
This year, NEVs’ share of sales has also bounced back from a low of 39% in January, after the full purchase tax exemption that had been in place for more than a decade came to an end in December 2025.
The gain in NEV share in 2026 has come amid a slowdown across the wider domestic passenger-car market, which has hit sales of combustion-engine vehicles particularly hard.
This September, passenger-car retail sales across all categories declined, with overall sales volumes falling 28% year-on-year.
The contraction was led by combustion-engine vehicles, which saw sales fall 43% year-on-year in September and 31% in 2026 to date.
However, sales of PHEVs also fell by 36% year-on-year in September and by 26% in 2026 to date. By comparison, BEVs performed better, although sales still declined 8.5% from a year earlier in September and 4% in 2026 to date.
As a result, NEV sales overall fell by 17% in September and 13% in 2026 to date.
While the market changes in 2026 to date were particularly dramatic, they reflect a broad continuation of trends seen over the past decade.
Indeed, sales of combustion-engine cars in China peaked in 2017 and they have been declining ever since, shown in the figure below.
Impact of Hormuz
Part of the reason for the advance of NEVs in 2026, said Chinese technology news outlet OFweek, was petrol cars “giving up market share” as they were outperformed by electric alternatives.
Cui Dongshu, secretary-general of the CPCA, cited higher petrol prices as an explanation for September’s weak combustion-car sales, in comments to financial news outlet National Business Daily.
Imports of oil into China in January-September have fallen 15% compared to 2025, equivalent to 470m barrels, as ongoing conflict tightened supply and drove up prices.
China’s passenger-car NEV fleet has displaced 143m barrels of oil so far during the strait of Hormuz crisis, Euan Graham, senior energy analyst at thinktank Ember, tells Carbon Brief.
EVs “accounted for 12% of the decrease in China’s oil use post-Hormuz”, according to an estimate provided to thinktank the Brookings Institute by an unnamed analyst.
Erica Downs, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, tells Carbon Brief that the strait of Hormuz crisis and higher oil prices are “reinforcing China’s electrification of road transport”.
She says the “world’s largest oil supply disruption” vindicates China’s early bet on EVs, which was partly driven by concerns about oil-supply security.
NEV demand down
Nevertheless, NEV sales have fallen year-on-year, albeit at a slower rate than overall car sales. The growth in NEV market share has also been decelerating.
Zhang Yichao, a partner at consulting firm AlixPartners, tells Carbon Brief that NEVs benefit from government trade-in policies and a “strong pipeline” of new models, particularly those involving innovation.
He says these factors help explain why NEVs sales have fallen at a slower rate to their combustion-car counterparts.
Cui told the state-run China National Radio that the fall for NEVs and for cars overall in September 2026, is also due to a high baseline of sales from the same month in 2025, as well as changes to trade-in policies and disruptions from the holiday period.
Other factors, says consulting firm Wood Mackenzie, are the weakened demand due to “demand pull-forward” in 2025 caused by the end of subsidies, as well as “tighter financing conditions”.
Zhang tells Carbon Brief he does not “see much more room ahead” for further growth in NEVs’ market share.
He adds that, in his view, their share in China is unlikely to exceed 80%, as some premium-market segments and specific use cases will continue to require combustion-engine vehicles.
Exports surge
Meanwhile, while domestic NEV retail sales fell 17% in September 2026, exports more than doubled, increasing 164% year-on-year, according to the CPCA.
This extends the decline in domestic sales and very strong growth in exports seen across 2026 to date, as shown in the figure below.
In September, 1,084,000 NEVs were sold domestically in China, while 558,000 NEVs were exported.
Exports are becoming increasingly important to Chinese carmakers, in the face of weaker domestic demand and cut-throat industrial competition.
The CPCA says exports have become “a core priority” for some carmakers.
However, the surge in exports from China has created concern in the EU, which has placed tariffs on imports of EVs from China and recently agreed plans to cut imports of hybrids.
Countries including Mexico and Turkey have also placed tariffs on Chinese EV imports.
At the same time, the Chinese government is putting policies in place that might be expected to disincentivise exports, such as cutting VAT export rebates.
Analysts differ on what impact this policy shift will have, with some saying it will be limited, while others believe it could cause the price of exported cars to rise.

A narrower expansion: Inside India’s startup funding recovery
Indian tech startups raised $10.94 billion in equity funding across 1,253 rounds between January 1 and October 15, 2026, up 7.1 per cent from $10.21 billion across 1,982 rounds in the corresponding period last year, according to Tracxn data.
The increase in funding value masks a sharper shift in how capital is being deployed. While the number of rounds fell 36.8 per cent year on year, the average funding per round rose from about $5.15 million in 2025 to $8.73 million in 2026.
The concentration of capital is particularly noticeable among the largest fundraisers. The top 10 fundraisers secured approximately $3.94 billion, accounting for 36 per cent of Indian tech startups’ total equity funding through 15 October 2026.
AI infrastructure startup Neysa secured up to $600 million in equity funding in February, while data center operator Nxtra announced a $1 billion investment in March. Fintech platform CRED raised approximately $540 million in June.
Inox Clean Energy raised a total of $417 million through investments recorded in January and July. Additionally, AI startup Sarvam secured around $345 million across funding rounds between June and August. Meanwhile, Rapido raised $240 million in May, fintech lender KreditBee obtained $220 million in April, and AI coding startup Emergent raised $200 million between January and July.
For venture capital investors, the pattern reflects a more selective market.
Vishesh Rajaram, managing partner at Speciale Invest, said the fall in round count alongside higher funding value points to capital pooling in companies that have moved beyond their first few rounds.
He cautioned, however, that seed-stage data can be reported with a lag, meaning the decline at the earliest stage may be overstated. Even with that caveat, he said, the bar for a first institutional cheque has risen.
“Much of this year’s capital is follow-on money into proven winners, which is sensible portfolio management but not new conviction,” he said. “The real test is the median early-stage cheque and how many companies raise their first round.”
Amit Chand, founder of BYT Capital, said higher funding values and fewer rounds do not necessarily mean investors are choosing established businesses at the expense of early-stage founders. The assessment of fundamentals, he said, differs by stage. In deeptech, founder expertise, differentiated technology, customer validation and a credible commercialisation plan can establish conviction before significant revenue comes in.
“Stronger conviction and follow-on funding can go hand in hand,” Chand said.
AI and deeptech attract attention, but concentration remains
Sector data points to a shift towards capital-intensive and technology-led businesses, even as other categories lose ground.
Early-stage investors backed fewer companies, but wrote larger cheques on average.
Anoop N Menon, partner at Chiratae Ventures, said the threshold for defensibility has risen. For AI-native companies, that means looking beyond a compelling demonstration or rapid user growth to proprietary workflows, contextual data, distribution and user experience that competitors cannot easily replicate.
“AI with vertical enterprise use cases is our big bet,” Menon said, pointing to opportunities in specialised applications where businesses can solve specific problems rather than rely on general-purpose AI alone.
He said Chiratae is also building positions in deeptech areas including spacetech, quantum, semiconductors and defence-adjacent technologies, alongside its investments in consumer, fintech and AI or software-as-a-service businesses.
Menon’s caution on traction also echoes Rajaram’s distinction between follow-on funding and new conviction. “Early traction proves that there is demand. It doesn't necessarily prove that there is an enduring company in the making,” Menon said. Growth can be driven by discounts, viral loops or high customer-acquisition spending without establishing retention, margins or pricing power.
That creates a challenge for founders in demonstrating progress, but not at the cost of building a business that depends on continual fundraising. Menon added that companies can scale go-to-market efforts faster than their product-market fit, organisational capabilities or financial discipline. By around series B, he said, enduring businesses often need to balance growth with unit economics, gross margins and customer payback periods.
The early-stage pipeline is the longer-term test
For Rajaram, a narrower funding funnel has consequences beyond the current fundraising cycle. “Depth comes from the number of new attempts, so a narrow funnel today means fewer breakout companies in five to seven years,” he said.
He argued that India’s ambitions in space, semiconductors, defence and energy require specialist funds and investors prepared to take early scientific risk and remain invested over a long period.
Recent funding rounds also highlight similar investor interest in India’s space tech sector. Pixxel raised $100 million in a Series C round last month, taking its total funding to $195 million, while Skyroot Aerospace raised $50 million in May, reaching a valuation of $1.1 billion. Other notable space tech funding rounds include Digantara’s $50 million series B and EtherealX’s $21 million series A.
Chand agreed that deeptech companies need investors who can recognise potential before revenue becomes substantial, and then provide additional capital as technical and commercial milestones are achieved. He said the ecosystem needs both a willingness to write the first cheque and the capacity to back companies through qualification, manufacturing and customer adoption.
The VCs suggest that India’s funding challenge is not simply about deploying more capital, but balancing discipline with risk-taking. As investors sharpen their focus on fundamentals and defensibility, the ecosystem must continue backing promising founders early while providing follow-on capital to companies that demonstrate meaningful technical and commercial progress.
“Global competitiveness depends on defensible IP, not India-specific workarounds, and a capital base that supports long R&D cycles rather than consumer-internet-style growth,” Menon argued.

indian-startups-95a97dccd8.headline: Zetwerk Makes Its Market Debut; Can Scale Alone Widen Its Thin Margins?
indian-startups-95a97dccd8.fulltext: Companies change course in good times and bad. For Zetwerk, the key turn came after it raised $150 Mn from D1 Capital Partners in August 2021 when Indian startups raised a record $42 Bn in the calendar year. And what began as a platform to connect manufacturers to vendors and suppliers, turned into a full stack manufacturing play on the back of a bevy of acquisitions in 2021 and 2022. The company, founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan and Vishal Chaudhary, made its stock market debut today (Friday, October 23) with that full-stack promise at the centre of its pitch. No longer is this a marketplace, but a full-fledged platform that manages everything from procurement, supply, manufacturing, specifications and delivery. While the listing itself was not at a massive premium like some other new-age tech stocks, that’s besides the point when looking at the business model and the sector. The thesis around manufacturing remains strong for years to come as companies in key segments such as electric vehicles are looking to bring more of their component sourcing to India including in vital areas like precision machined parts. This was the opportunity that Zetwerk wanted to capture with its shift from marketplace to manufacturing. In FY26, its revenue from operations rose 40.4% YoY to ₹15,913 Cr, from ₹11,331 Cr in the previous fiscal. Yet, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606 Cr from ₹371 Cr in FY25. This loss includes an exceptional charge of ₹836 Cr from continuing operations and a ₹453 Cr impairment related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business. Those are the realities of working in the manufacturing space. Opportunities come and go and companies have to react in terms of pivoting their operations. The impairment itself is not a major number, but what could worry investors is that adjusted EBITDA stood at a mere ₹421 Cr, translating into a margin of just 2.65% against the revenue. Plus, cash flows present another challenge. Zetwerk’s cash outflow from operations widened to ₹682 Cr in FY26 from ₹386 Cr a year earlier, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.4% to ₹12,370 Cr. A larger order book offers revenue visibility, but fulfilling those orders requires the company to fund procurement, production and logistics, while managing payments to suppliers and collections from customers. Let’s dive deeper into this as this is what investors will look at. The Two Revenue Pillars Zetwerk operates through two main business segments: manufacturing and ecosystem. The latter operates under the Terra91 brand and supplies industrial raw materials such as steel, aluminium, copper, zinc, lead and bitumen. The manufacturing business, which focuses on custom-made industrial products and related projects, is the largest of the two. Together, the two businesses generated ₹15,913 Cr in revenue from continuing operations in FY26, up 40.4% YoY. Manufacturing accounted for ₹9,375 Cr, or 58.9% of revenue, while ecosystem contributed ₹6,539 Cr, or 41.1%. Simply put, the manufacturing business earns revenue by working with third-party manufacturers and Zetwerk’s own facilities to fulfil orders across energy products, precision machined products and capital goods. Its earnings depend on the price charged to customers relative to supplier payments, materials and fulfilment costs. More complex work, such as precision manufacturing requiring tight tolerances, can command a higher take rate than relatively less complex products. Notably, Zetwerk doesn’t disclose these margins and fees as it is likely to depend on the product and client needs, since this is how the industry functions. In an earlier Inc42 interview, cofounder and CEO Acharya said the company does not consider commission when accounting for revenue. He described the model instead as a take rate for services. He said rates vary across product categories depending on the complexity of the work. The manufacturing segment reported a standalone EBITDA of ₹565 Cr in FY26, translating into a margin of 6.03%. The other side is the ecosystem, which has grown considerably since 2022 as we indicated in the beginning. Unlike manufacturing, where Zetwerk coordinates production, the ecosystem segment aggregates demand for industrial raw materials, procures them in bulk and resells them to customers. Its economics are driven by the spread between procurement and selling prices, after accounting for logistics and other fulfillment costs. The segment’s Adjusted EBITDA stood at around ₹81 Cr, giving it a margin of approximately 1.24%. The thin margin means that changes in commodity prices, sourcing costs or delivery expenses can have a significant impact on profitability, which we will see soon. Plus, the margin is considerably thinner than in manufacturing. These segment-level margins offer a view of Zetwerk’s economics, but the company has not disclosed commission rates or order-level profitability. Zetwerk’s revenue from operations includes the sale of products, income from construction and project contracts, sale of services and other operating revenue. Product sales cover manufactured goods, products sourced from third-party suppliers and industrial raw materials sold through the ecosystem business. Construction and project contract income relates to projects involving broader execution responsibilities, while service revenue includes activities such as job work and related services. Here’s the key difference from any other marketplace: Zetwerk acts as the principal in these transactions rather than simply connecting buyers and suppliers for a fee. It takes responsibility for sourcing, quality and delivery, meaning the revenue it reports reflects the value of goods and services sold, while procurement and fulfillment costs are recorded separately. This is precisely the turn that Zetwerk’s 2021 fundraise and subsequent expansion allowed. Zetwerk’s Big Opportunity Having said that, as we mentioned in the beginning, the problem for the company is that it operates with razor thin margins. Even as the adjusted EBITDA margin has improved year-on-year, it’s still not quite robust enough. Fulfilling industrial orders starts with a substantial procurement bill and procurement costs almost always escalate when there is a disparity in the order book. The key thing for Zetwerk will be to double down in one or two categories which will allow it to maximise the arbitrage revenue. Economies of scale will drive arbitrage revenue in the manufacturing business, especially when Zetwerk owns and controls the procurement side of the business. So manufacturing cannot drive profits on its own and Zetwerk will have to flesh out both sides of the business at the same time. Owning procurement removes third-party broker fees, distributor markups, and structural inefficiencies. The company captures the full margin that middle-men usually take. Add to that, sourcing inputs from low-cost regions which allows you to absorb fixed costs of logistics, customs, and compliance. And as the procurement side of the business scales up, Zetwerk will also have leverage for exclusive, long-term low-price contracts. But it’s not a flick of the switch, buying in extreme bulk can exponentially increase warehousing, insurance, and inventory carrying costs. Moreover, commodity price volatility is another factor since companies can get locked in to massive forward contracts even as market price shifts. So any arbitrage advantage gets flipped here. In FY26, the company spent ₹9,880 Cr on purchases of stock-in-trade and another ₹3,964 Cr on materials consumed, making these its two largest expense heads. Together, they accounted for nearly 86% of its total expenses of ₹16,142 Cr. Purchases of stock-in-trade largely represent goods bought from suppliers and resold to customers. This expense head rose 45.3% YoY to ₹9,880 Cr in FY26 from ₹6,800 Cr in the previous fiscal. The cost of materials consumed includes materials used in manufacturing and project contracts — which increased 31% YoY to ₹3,964 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,036 Cr. The two expense heads reflect the procurement-heavy nature of Zetwerk’s business, where revenue growth requires the company to source goods, materials and manufacturing capacity to meet customer orders. Why Revenue Growth Is Not Translating Into Cash Zetwerk’s cash flow numbers point to the pressure of achieving the balance between procurement and manufacturing. In FY26, its net cash outflow from operating activities widened to ₹682 Cr from ₹386 Cr in FY25, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.3% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹12,370 Cr. A growing order book provides visibility into future business, but it does not immediately translate into cash in the bank. Zetwerk still needs to source materials, pay suppliers and coordinate production to fulfil orders, while customer payments may come in only after goods are delivered or project milestones are met. This gap between spending on fulfillment and collecting revenue can tie up cash as the business expands. The company’s procurement-heavy model means it’s particularly important that Zetwerk gets this balance right. As order volumes rise, the company may need to deploy more working capital to support the procurement, manufacturing and fulfillment needs, even if each order itself is profitable. The challenge is therefore not simply to grow revenue or expand the order book, but to wring out inefficiencies in terms of arbitrage price, production bottlenecks and generally save costs through tech and AI. This will help the company mitigate the risks of delayed cash inflows and receivables. In FY26, Zetwerk’s trade receivables increased by ₹336 Cr, while its other financial and current assets rose by ₹715 Cr. Zetwerk’s ability to improve cash conversion will depend on how efficiently it manages inventory, supplier terms, production timelines, fulfillment and customer collections as it scales. Converting the order book pipeline into cash remains a big test of its business model. Which is why Zetwerk is looking to capture more value by taking on design and engineering responsibilities, rather than simply manufacturing products to customer specifications. Its original design manufacturing (ODM) contracts accounted for 13.93% of manufacturing gross merchandise value (GMV) in FY26. Such work can offer better margins because it involves design and co-development, while also making customer relationships harder to replace. Zetwerk is also trying to balance its supplier network with greater control over complex manufacturing. It operated 26 manufacturing facilities across four countries as of June 2026, while continuing to rely on third-party manufacturers for most of its manufacturing business. Products sourced from third-party suppliers accounted for 80.46% of manufacturing segment revenue in FY26, down from 96.51% in FY24. This suggests that Zetwerk is gradually reducing its dependence on external capacity, but has not moved away from the model that helped it scale without investing in every stage of production. But is scale alone enough to improve profitability? And now as a public company, Zetwerk will have to answer this tricky question.

indian-startups-60f5419e6d.headline: IPO-Bound Garuda Aerospace’s FY26 Profit Jumps 41% To ₹25.9 Cr
indian-startups-60f5419e6d.fulltext: Chennai-based dronetech startup Garuda Aerospace reported a net profit of ₹25.9 Cr in FY26, growing 41.1% from ₹18.4 Cr from the previous fiscal year. In terms of operational profitability, the drone maker’s EBITA for the fiscal year jumped 31.8% to ₹35.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹26.6 Cr in the FY25. Operating revenue surged 66.8% YoY to ₹206 Cr during the fiscal under review from ₹123.5 Cr in the previous year. Sales of drones and drone parts brought in ₹99.4 Cr to the top line while the remaining ₹106.5 Cr via sale of services. Another ₹15 Lakh was earned from delivery charges. Including other income of ₹26.5 Lakh, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹206.2 Cr. “During the year, we continued to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, expand our Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) operations, deepen our investment in indigenous research and development, and build strategic partnerships in India and international markets. We also advanced our capabilities in artificial intelligence, autonomous flight, data analytics, defence systems and specialised mission platforms,” cofounder and whole-time director Agnishwar Jayaprakash noted in a message to shareholders. The improvement in the financial performance comes as Garuda’s proposed public listing plans take shape. The startup took the pre-filing route to confidentially submit its draft IPO papers with the SEBI earlier in April. The IPO was greenlit by the markets regulator in August. While the startup is yet to file its updated DRHP for public access, its board approved plans to raise up to ₹750 Cr via the fresh issue component of the proposed IPO back in March. As per reports, the OFS component could result in investors offloading shares worth as much as ₹250 Cr. In its annual report for FY26, the startup disclosed that its board of directors had approved a private placement of equity shares worth ₹57.2 Cr back in August. Investors who backed the startup were Umasankar Nistala, Rakesh Pillai, Jitendra Rana, Vimaan Innovators LLP and Aditum Management. The proceeds of the issue would fuel business growth, working capital requirements, and be used for loan repayments. The startup claims to have become India’s largest drone maker, having manufactured and sold over 3000 drones. It also claimed to be the first drone company to partner with three defence PSUs. It has raised a total funding of over $37 Mn to date from investors like Venture Catalysts, We Founder Circle, cricketer Mahendra Singh Dhoni, among others. It was last valued at $250 Mn after raising a $11 Mn Series B funding round led by Venture Catalysts. Where Did Garuda Aerospace Spend In FY26? Garuda Aerospace’s total expenses in FY26 rose 73.2% YoY to ₹172.2 Cr from ₹99.4 Cr in FY25. It reported no exceptional items during the fiscal but bore ₹8.2 Cr tax expenses. Here are the main operational expenses of the startup: Cost of Materials Consumed: Representing the largest operational expense, raw material costs surged 61.5% YoY to ₹116.8 Cr from ₹72.3 Cr in FY25. Impairment Losses on Financial Assets: Impairment losses amounted to ₹11.1 Cr in FY26, compared to ₹6.5 Lakh in the year-ago period. Employee Benefit Expenses: Garuda Aerospace’s personnel-related costs decreased 16.7% YoY to ₹8 Cr in FY26 from ₹9.6 Cr in the previous year. Depreciation And Amortisation Expenses: The cost recorded under this line item increased 13.3% YoY to ₹4.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹3.6 Cr in FY25. Other Expenses: Spending on items like professional expenses, travel, maintenance, rent, and other corporate overheads stayed nearly flat at ₹29.2 Cr.

Chinese artificial intelligence chip giant Cambricon Technologies reported a 147.7 per cent surge in third-quarter profit on Friday, as the country’s aggressive push to replace Nvidia chips continues to fuel high growth among local chipmakers.
The Shanghai-listed chipmaker generated 1.4 billion yuan (US$210 million) in net profit for the three months ended September 30, up from 566.6 million yuan during the same period last year.
Revenue reached 3.5 billion yuan, an increase of 104.5 per cent from a year ago, according to its stock exchange filing. That was faster than the company’s 75.8 per cent revenue increase seen in the second quarter.
Cambricon attributed the revenue surge to its continuous market expansion and efforts to “facilitate the implementation of AI applications”. This top-line increase directly drove the year-on-year surge in total profit and net profit, the company said in the filing.
Shares of Cambricon closed up 5.5 per cent at 932.2 yuan ahead of the earnings release on Friday.
Earlier this week, Hygon Information Technology, another leading domestic AI chipmaker, posted third-quarter revenue of 5.9 billion yuan, an increase of 45.5 per cent year on year. Its net profit for the quarter surged 37.9 per cent year on year to 1 billion yuan.
The momentum at Cambricon and Hygon builds on Beijing’s initiative to develop a self-sufficient AI computing ecosystem, as the country accelerates the deployment of AI infrastructure powered by home-grown chips.
The two companies – regarded as top-tier players in the domestic AI chip sector – are moving rapidly to fill the market vacuum left by Washington’s export controls that have cut off China’s access to advanced AI accelerators from US chip giants like Nvidia.
Analysts said Cambricon’s earnings outlook depended largely on the commercialisation progress of its latest chips, which was in turn affected by supply chain pressures, especially the shortage of high bandwidth memory chips required for AI data centres.
“Cambricon delivered [its] MLU692 to a major cloud service provider in Q3 for testing, but we expect most revenue to be recognised in Q4,” Morgan Stanley analysts wrote in a recent research report. “MLU580 shipments also remain limited as higher high bandwidth memory costs pressure unit economics.”
The MLU692 is part of Cambricon’s MLU690 chip series, also known as Siyuan 690. The series can outperform Nvidia’s H20 by 50 to 150 per cent when measured in “tokens per second”, a metric that essentially counts how many words or other data AI can process and spit out, according to an earlier Morgan Stanley report.
Hygon, meanwhile, faces high expectations for its next-generation central processing unit and its deep computing unit – a type of accelerator card designed specifically for AI.
The company said on Thursday that the progress was “on track” with key metrics such as compute density and interconnect bandwidth set to be upgraded, though mass production timelines remained pending.
Ann Cao is a Shanghai-based technology reporter for the Post, covering technology start-ups and policies in the city and eastern China. She graduated from the University of Hong Kong with a master's degree in journalism.

climate-energy-fe5f84563f.fulltext:
The real test of India’s carbon market is getting the price right
In today’s geopolitical and trade landscape, a credible domestic carbon price is not just climate policy, but an industrial strategy as well
Visual Credits: Arkatapa Basu
India is putting a national price on industrial carbon for the first time. Under the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), baselines and final targets have been notified for seven energy-intensive sectors covering roughly 490 industrial emitters. The world’s sixth largest economy is joining a global shift: emissions trading systems now cover about 28% of the world's emissions and have raised more than $100 billion a year through auction revenues and other forms of carbon pricing.
The debate so far was about whether India should have a carbon market. That is now settled. The harder one is whether the market India builds will actually work.
A new report from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) and Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), examines precisely that, drawing on the experiences from carbon markets in the EU, South Korea, China and the state of California in the US. The report’s central conclusion is that getting the price signal right in the early years will be critical in building confidence and credibility in the market over time.
One should start with why the price matters at all. The whole purpose of a carbon market is to incentivise emission reductions. International assessments estimate that a single tonne of carbon dioxide inflicts around $140-380 (₹13,000-₹36,000) of damage on society — through worse health, lower farm yields and harsher weather. An unregulated emitter pays none of it.
A carbon market exists to close that gap. If the price it produces is weak, the gap stays open, and the market becomes less effective.
India's carbon market design is deliberate. Rather than setting a single absolute ceiling on emissions, as Europe does, it has chosen an intensity-based system in which firms are judged on emissions per tonne of output, not against a national cap. That lets an economy growing at 6.6% to 6.8% a year keep expanding without the carbon limit constraining production levels.
Also Read: Can biochar be India’s missing link to carbon capture?
It is the right instrument for a country that still has to industrialise. Underpinning all of this, credits are issued only after a firm's performance is verified. While this design has much to commend it, it also raises a challenge that merits a wider conversation.
A fine balance
In an intensity-based market, economic growth can create both buyers and sellers of credits. Firms that outperform their emissions-intensity targets generate credits that they can sell, while firms that fall short must buy them. The balance between supply and demand therefore depends on how ambitious the targets are and which firms are expanding production.
Carbon scarcity does not emerge automatically; it is created through policy design. Set the benchmarks too generously, and the market fills with cheap credits that reward business-as-usual and send little signal to invest in cleaner technologies. Set them too tightly, and firms face costs they may not yet be able to absorb.
This is not a theoretical worry. Historical experience offers a useful lesson. Europe's carbon market, for example, struggled with low carbon prices in its initial phases, prompting a series of reforms to strengthen the market. It issued too many permits, prices fell close to zero, and for the better part of a decade, the market did little to cut emissions.
Asia has similar stories: in their early phases, carbon prices sat below $10 in South Korea and between $6-$8 in China, drifting up to only around $14 by late 2024 — numbers set more by administrative design than by real scarcity. The lesson is blunt: a carbon market is only as strong as the scarcity built into it.
There is a hard commercial reason to get this right, too. From 2026, the EU's carbon border tax will require importers of steel, aluminum and other goods to pay for the emissions embedded in them, in line with EU carbon prices. If India does not price its own industrial carbon credibly, that bill will simply be collected in Brussels. In today’s geopolitical and trade landscape, a credible domestic carbon price is not just climate policy, but an industrial strategy as well.
Learning curve
The good news is that India can choose not to repeat these mistakes. It also starts with a foundation: for more than a decade, the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme has familiarised energy-intensive industries with compliance obligations, third-party verification, and tradable certificates. While a carbon market is a different instrument, these experiences provide a valuable starting point.
Three priorities stand out.
The first is a predictable tightening path. A blast furnace or a cement kiln locks in emissions for 15 to 30 years. No firm will price carbon into a thirty-year decision unless it believes the targets will tighten steadily and will not be quietly relaxed the moment industry pushes back. Europe, having learned the hard way, now follows a predictable annual reduction in the number of emission allowances available to the market. The rate of decline increased from 1.7% to 2.2% from 2021 onwards, steadily tightening supply and strengthening the carbon price signal. Publishing a clear, long-term trajectory of this kind is the single most powerful signal the government can send.
Also Read: What can India’s bilateral carbon credit deals learn from the centralised global carbon market?
The second is a stability mechanism built in from the outset. Rather than responding to challenges after they arise, India can strengthen market confidence by embedding appropriate safeguards from the outset. Europe recovered only after it created an automatic rule that reduces the supply of tradable emission allowances when surpluses build up. A transparent, rule-based version should be built into the CCTS too.
The third is a thoughtful roadmap for sectoral expansion. Currently, the CCTS roughly covers 20% of India’s emissions. The immediate priority is not to maximize coverage overnight, but to make the initial design work well. At the same time, policymakers should start signaling how the market would expand over time to cover a larger share of the economy. Wider sectoral coverage can deepen the market, increase opportunities for cost-effective abatement, and strengthen the carbon price signal.
Also Read: India Has Potential to Build $45 Billion Biochar Carbon Removal Market by 2030: Report
Need for expansion
Market depth matters too. Today, participation is largely limited to obligated entities. In more mature carbon markets, financial institutions also participate, providing liquidity by matching buyers and sellers, helping firms manage price risk, and supporting more continuous trading. While limiting participation in the early years is understandable, greater clarity on whether and how market participation could broaden over time would help firms and investors plan ahead.
Both are sensible evolutionary steps rather than immediate requirements. The objective is not to make the market bigger for its own sake, but to provide a clear sense of direction for how the CCTS can mature as India's carbon market develops.
There is a quieter risk as well. India is running many climate and industrial policies at once, including renewable consumption obligations, efficiency mandates, production-linked incentives, the Green Hydrogen Mission, the Green Credit Programme and others. Each is valuable. But where they cut emissions in the very sectors the carbon market covers, they can drain demand for credits and depress the price, with no one intending it. The carbon market must sit at the centre of this architecture, with the rest calibrated to reinforce its signal, not undercut it. That calls for coordination across ministries, states and regulators.
None of these is a case for hesitation. It is the opposite. As IEEFA and EDF’s analysis makes clear, a well-built CCTS could become one of the most powerful tools India has to reach net zero by 2070 while keeping its industry competitive — steering capital toward the firms and technologies that pollute the least and turning a cost on carbon into an advantage for the cleanest.
But a market is only as good as the price it produces, and a price is only as good as the promise behind it. Europe learned that at great cost. Asia is still learning it. India, building with all of it in plain view, has the rare chance to get it right the first time.

India
'Is another Galwan unfolding?': Congress targets PM Modi over reported PLA face-offs in Arunachal
Opposition raises concerns over national security and surging trade deficit with Beijing, calling for transparency on Line of Actual Control developments.
The Congress on Friday accused the Centre of remaining silent on reports of continuing face-offs between Indian and Chinese forces in Arunachal Pradesh, demanding answers from Prime Minister Narendra Modi on border security and India's diplomatic approach towards Beijing.
The allegations followed reported remarks by Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapoor about recent confrontations with China's People's Liberation Army (PLA). The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), responding to questions on the remarks, said Chinese forces sometimes diverged from established patrolling patterns along the border.
"Insofar as the specifics are concerned, I would refer you to the Ministry of Defence. As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," the MEA spokesperson said.
The spokesperson said both countries continued to use diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and prevent misunderstandings along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
"Both sides continue to use existing diplomatic and military mechanisms to resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstanding and miscalculation along the Line of Actual Control (LAC). The two sides have also agreed to discuss ways to improve understanding of the LAC in appropriate areas for better border management. I would also like to emphasise that the maintenance of peace and tranquillity in the border areas is essential for the overall development of bilateral relations," the spokesperson added.
Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge led the opposition's criticism, arguing that the government had given Beijing "enough clean chits" and demanding accountability over the border situation.
In a post on X, Kharge raised questions about national security, India's economic dependence on China and the outcome of diplomatic engagement between the two countries.
"The ITBP DG's confirmation of continuing PLA face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh is deeply alarming. After Doklam and Galwan, is another serious confrontation unfolding? Reports of Chinese incursions near Taksing emerged in August. Yet, even 47 days after Corps Commander-level talks at Wacha–Damai, reportedly just 180 km away, confrontations continue. Has India's patrolling access been compromised?" Kharge asked.
He said national security required accountability rather than "diplomatic photo opportunities and Hugplomacy".
Kharge also criticised the rise in Chinese imports and India's trade deficit with Beijing.
"Since the Galwan sacrifice of 20 Indian Army bravehearts (FY2020–21), Chinese imports have surged 102%, while India's trade deficit with China has ballooned 155% to $112.16 billion... Has Make in India become Import from China?" he said.
Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh also accused the government of making concessions to China while failing to address the reported face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh.
"While the self-styled Vishwaguru’s calibrated concessions to China continue, the DG, ITBP, has lauded—and rightly so—its performance in recent face-offs with the PLA in Arunachal Pradesh, on which there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Ramesh posted on X.
Ramesh also flagged China's renaming of places in Arunachal Pradesh and the construction of a 60,000-MW dam on the Brahmaputra, warning of potential consequences for India's ecological and water security.
At a press conference at the All India Congress Committee (AICC) headquarters, Congress leader Pawan Khera accused the government of compromising India's interests out of fear of Beijing. He questioned whether Indian forces retained access to traditional patrolling points and raised concerns about the easing of visa restrictions for Chinese personnel and the removal of investment curbs under Press Note 3.
"What did we get? Can we patrol the points today where we used to patrol before April 2020, or not? In exchange for all this, shouldn't you have taken something? Or did you just accept that you will do whatever China wants because you are afraid?" Khera asked.
Referring to videos from border villages in Arunachal Pradesh, Khera said residents had been raising concerns about Chinese incursions.
"Every day you hear that China has entered Arunachal; local rural people are making emotional appeals on social media... Tell the DG of ITBP that everything is normal. Tell those 20 families whose people were martyred that everything is normal," he said.
Congress MP Jebi Mather questioned why the reported confrontations had not been disclosed to the public earlier, noting that the ITBP chief's remarks suggested the incidents had been occurring since July.
"The ITBP Director General has made a very strong revelation... but the fact is he is saying this has been happening since July, which means we are in October and now it took for the nation to know about this when an ITBP Director General revealed it. We have not heard anything about this from our Prime Minister. We have not heard anything about this from our Home Minister," Mather said.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Priyanka Chaturvedi also called on the government's senior security leadership to explain the apparent gap between diplomatic statements and developments along the border.
Speaking to ANI, Chaturvedi said, "It is the responsibility of the country’s Home Minister, Defence Minister, and Minister of External Affairs to provide an answer. On one hand, we keep talking about trying to normalize relations with China—implying that all is well—yet, on the other hand, there is a persistent pattern of such statements being made, time and again. Given that this concerns the nation’s security, its sensitive interests, and the national interest, those responsible must be held accountable.”
Communist Party of India (CPI) general secretary D Raja urged Modi to focus on national security issues instead of criticising political opponents.
"Prime Minister Modi should realise he is the Prime Minister of India. Instead of resorting to cheap rhetoric against opposition leaders like Rahul Gandhi, he must speak on the real issues facing the country today," Raja said.
He expressed confidence that the two countries could resolve their differences through dialogue.
"Both are neighbouring countries with cooperation in multiple fields. Whatever the disputes which appear, both countries have that maturity, have their experience to sort out, resolve through dialogue," he added.
Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke also criticised the Centre's security priorities, alleging that security forces were being deployed to prevent protests in Delhi instead of focusing on border protection.
"Yeah, because forces that should be protecting our borders are being deployed to stop citizens from protesting. Modi is putting national security at risk by using security forces against his own countrymen. The priority should be securing our borders, not deploying forces to turn Delhi into a fortress to suppress peaceful citizen protests," Dipke posted on X.
(With inputs from ANI)

Romania blames Russia after drone sinks ship in the Black Sea
One sailor killed and three others missing after Comoros-flagged Khoryv hit near Romanian waters.
Romania has blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship off Romania’s Black Sea coast, killing one crew member and leaving three others missing.
It’s the latest drone attack targeting commercial shipping off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and 30 sailors reported killed or missing in the past two weeks, raising fears of an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The drone struck the Comoros-flagged vessel Khoryv and its crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors on Friday, 13 nautical miles (24km) off Romania’s port of Constanta, just outside Romania’s territorial waters.
The shipping data website MarineTraffic showed the Khoryv departed Turkiye on Wednesday and was headed for Romania’s Sulina port, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea.
The canal has become the primary route for Ukrainian exporters, which rely on ports on the Danube and Romanian territorial waters, as Russia has attacked Ukraine’s own Black Sea ports.
Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above the waves as it sank.
Romania launched a rescue operation after the Khoryv sent a distress signal about 10am local time (0700 GMT).
Nine sailors were rescued, three were missing and one body was recovered during a search and rescue operation hampered by poor weather conditions and low visibility, Romania’s naval authority said.
Drone attack surge in the Black Sea
Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to “fast-track the additional surveillance capabilities” to protect commercial shipping, after a surge in Black Sea drone attacks as fighting in Russia’s war on Ukraine escalates. NATO said on Tuesday that it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.
Romanian and European officials blamed Russia for the attack, which Romania’s President Nicusor Dan called “a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine”.
“It is time for Russia to take peace initiatives of the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war,” he said.
Romania’s Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Facebook that the attack was “unacceptable and constitutes a flagrant violation of international law”.
Moldova’s Foreign Ministry posted on X that “Russia’s continued escalation in the Black Sea endangers civilian lives, threatens freedom of navigation and undermines regional security”.
EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the attacks “reckless”, which “target innocent lives and openly defy international law.”
Russian officials did not immediately publicly comment on Friday’s sinking. It occurred after Romanian warplanes shot down two of the latest-generation Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters on Saturday. Russia has previously denied it is responsible for deadly drone attacks in the region.
