other-interests-e8b987c95a.headline: Brazil presidential election dogged by alleged bias by Meta AI tools
other-interests-e8b987c95a.fulltext:
A deluge of AI-generated content and unfair treatment by social media platforms could prove pivotal in Brazil’s presidential election, according to supporters of the left-wing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
Lula will face off against right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro on 25 October in the second round of the contest. Lula’s campaign has formally accused Meta – which owns WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook – of favouring Bolsonaro by suspending Lula’s campaign advertising account, suppressing posts and blocking AI-generated content.
Brazil’s electoral prosecutors have said Meta failed to fully comply with court orders to ensure equal treatment of both candidates, while United Nations human rights experts have said they are concerned by possible unequal treatment of the two campaigns.
Advertisement
Images have widely circulated showing Meta AI, a chatbot integrated into WhatsApp, refusing to generate campaign posters for Lula, while instantly producing an image for “Flávio”.
In a statement, Meta said “claims that we are favoring or interfering on behalf of any candidate or political group are false and unfounded”. It said Lula’s account was suspended for 1 hour by mistake and that its systems blocked prompts referring to the names “Lula” and “Bolsonaro”, but not the common first names Luiz or Flávio.
Lula’s campaign remains unconvinced. It submitted screenshots to the electoral court showing Meta AI repeatedly assigning Bolsonaro’s electoral number, 22, to generic, fictional politicians and allegedly translating “Flávio futuro presidiário” (“Flávio future prisoner”) as “Flávio future president”.
Determining whether the discrepancies are deliberate is impossible because Meta’s systems are opaque, says David Nemer at the University of Virginia. “But when a technical glitch tends to repeat its outcome, it’s very hard to accept that this is just a technical failure.”
Lula finished behind Bolsonaro in the first round of voting, but polls show the gap is narrowing. The comeback has been partly credited to Lula’s Army, an intensive online campaign in which 8 million WhatsApp channel subscribers receive daily tasks, such as posting photographs on Instagram posing with their fingers forming an L.
This year’s general election is Brazil’s first since large language models (LLMs) became widely popular, and it is awash with AI-generated content. Experts say Latin America’s largest democracy offers a glimpse of what is to come for AI in politics.
Fact-checking organisation Lupa identified 920 pieces of AI-generated or manipulated election content ahead of the first round, primarily on Facebook and Instagram, 60 per cent of it unlabelled. Another investigation found that 26 Meta advertising accounts appeared to sidestep restrictions on foreign-funded political advertising by posting AI-generated videos, including one depicting Bolsonaro and Argentina’s president Javier Milei freeing Brazil from communists.
Meta’s independent oversight board says the company’s election safeguards have failed.
“It’s very worrying,” says Nemer. “So much of our political campaign dynamics have been transferred to privatised companies that we have no idea how they operate.”
Regulating AI in political campaigns won’t be as simple as it seems, says Heloísa Massaro at InternetLab, a Brazilian digital rights non-profit that studied how eight major AI chatbots respond to questions about Brazil’s election.
Its report found that chatbots sometimes refused genuine questions about candidates, referring users to official electoral websites, but would agree to draft misleading claims questioning the integrity of elections for use in campaigning.
Massaro says clearer safeguards for LLMs are needed, but first their objectives must be defined.
“Are the safeguards working? That’s one question. But working for what, because it depends on what your goals are,” she says. “Is the solution to send people away without providing any kind of information? Is this what we want?”

india-2af34a88de.headline: India slashes cost of cancer drugs after court rules mark-ups are ‘extortion’
india-2af34a88de.fulltext:
The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

indian-startups-386c83896b.headline: Garuda Aerospace’s FY26 revenue jumps 67% to Rs 206 Cr; profit rise 42%
indian-startups-386c83896b.fulltext:
Drone technology startup Garuda Aerospace reported a strong 67% year-on-year revenue growth in FY26 while maintaining profitability, with net profit at Rs 26 crore as the Chennai-based company is preparing to go public soon as it recently received SEBI nod for Rs 1,000 crore IPO.
Garuda’s revenue from operations rose to Rs 206 crore in the fiscal year ended March 2026,compared to Rs 123.5 crore in FY25, according to its financial statements filed with the Registrar of Companies (RoC).
Garuda Aerospace designs and manufactures drones for applications across agriculture, defence, infrastructure, mining and disaster management. Besides drone manufacturing, the firm also offers Drone-as-a-Service (DaaS) and operates a DGCA-approved remote pilot training programme. 
Revenue from sale of services surged 84.1% to Rs 106.46 crore in FY26 from Rs 57.83 crore in FY25, while revenue from sale of products grew 66.2% to Rs 99.50 crore from Rs 59.85 crore during the same period.
On the expense front, the cost of materials, remains the largest expense component, rose 62% to Rs 117 crore in FY26 from Rs 72.21 crore in FY25. Meanwhile, employee benefit expenses declined 16.2% to Rs 8 crore from Rs 9.55 crore.
Legal and professional charges surged 94.6% to Rs 12.88 crore from Rs 6.62 crore. Other overheads such as impairment loss on financial assets, depreciation & amortization expenses, travelling added another Rs 34.12 crore to the total cost.
Overall, Garuda’s total expenses grew 73.7% to Rs 172 crore in the last fiscal year compared to Rs 99 crore in FY25.
Despite the increase in costs, the company reported a 41.5% increase in net profit to Rs 26 crore in FY26 from Rs 18.37 crore in FY25. Its return on capital employed (ROCE) stood and EBITDA margin stood  at 14.71% and 18.97% respectively.
On a unit level, Garuda spent Rs 0.83 to generate every rupee of operating revenue in FY26, compared to Rs 0.80 in FY25. 
At the end of March 2026, the firm’s total current assets increased to Rs 303 crore from Rs 176 crore, while its cash and bank balance stood at Rs 5.2 crore.
Garuda Aerospace pre-filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with SEBI through the confidential route in April. The proposed Rs 1,000 crore IPO comprises a fresh issue of shares worth Rs 750 crore and an offer for sale (OFS) of Rs 250 crore by existing shareholders.

climate-energy-2ea2c14ddb.fulltext:
India’s Solar Wafer Expansion Faces Utilization and Cost Challenges: Interview
High financing costs and polysilicon import dependence pose challenges for domestic manufacturers
October 23, 2026
Follow Mercom India on WhatsApp for exclusive updates on clean energy news and insights
India’s planned expansion of solar ingot and wafer manufacturing capacity could lead to oversupply unless production growth aligns with domestic demand and exports.
Agastya Energy has announced plans to invest approximately ₹78 billion (~$826.46 million) in a 12 GW ingot and wafer manufacturing facility at Orvakal in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh. The project is expected to generate more than 3,500 jobs and complement the company’s planned 5 GW solar cell and module manufacturing capacity.
With India’s ingot and wafer capacity projected to reach approximately 80 GW by June 2028, manufacturers face challenges related to capacity utilization, production costs, import dependence, and global competitiveness.
In an interview with Mercom India, Bernhard Rack, CEO of Agastya Energy, discussed the risks of overcapacity, cost disadvantages compared with Chinese manufacturers, the implications of ALMM List-III, and India’s prospects as a solar wafer exporter.
With India’s ingot and wafer capacity expanding ahead of the 2028 ALMM mandate, is there a risk of oversupply? What utilization would a 12 GW facility need to remain globally competitive?
Yes, the risk is real. Official projections point to around 80 GW of ingot and wafer capacity by June 2028. The demand that matters is operating cell capacity that can qualify and consume those wafers, and that is ultimately bound by installations and exports. India installed a record of nearly 45 GW last financial year. We have watched module capacity run ahead of demand; we should not repeat that upstream.
Ingots and wafers are far more capital-intensive than modules, so utilization decides everything. To be globally competitive, a 12 GW plant needs to run consistently at 80–85% of saleable output. At 60%, fixed cost per watt is 50% higher than at 85%.
Where will the biggest cost gaps between Indian and Chinese wafers remain, and what would it take to close them?
Not in labor, and over time, not in yield. Indian engineers will close the yield and silicon-consumption gaps within a few years of running. Learning curves can be climbed.
The gaps that persist are structural: the cost of capital, the cost of power and the depth of the supplier ecosystem. Chinese producers finance plants more cheaply, run pullers on low-cost power and source consumables nearby. Buying the same equipment does not buy the same operating economics. Closing the gap needs round-the-clock renewable power at competitive tariffs, long-tenor financing for upstream assets and consumables localized around manufacturing clusters.
Which upstream inputs will India continue to import despite localizing ingot and wafer manufacturing? Which dependency poses the greatest strategic risk?
Localizing ingots and wafers moves the dependency upstream; it does not remove it. In the near term, almost all polysilicon, most quartz crucibles, diamond wire and the bulk of pullers and wire saws will be imported, largely from China. Graphite parts and process gases are easier to localize.
The biggest strategic risk is polysilicon. It is the largest single cost input; India has no commercial production yet, and more than 90% of global supply sits in one country. It also determines traceability. Close behind is equipment: a puller without spare parts and service support is an expensive idle asset.
How can manufacturers future-proof a 12 GW facility against evolving wafer sizes, thicknesses, and cell technologies?
The semiconductor industry learned, in the move from 200 mm to 300 mm, that the wrong format can strand an entire fab. In solar, the lock-in sits mainly in the hot zone and ingot diameter, less in slicing.
The principles are simple. Choose pullers that can grow the larger diameters the roadmap points to, so today’s formats and tomorrow’s come from the same platform. Go thinner where saleable yield and cell performance justify it, not for silicon savings alone. Design for quality, because back-contact and tandem cells will demand longer lifetimes and tighter oxygen control. Building in phases lets each tranche take the latest equipment.
Where will the first major supply-demand mismatch emerge in India’s solar manufacturing value chain, and how will it affect margins?
The first mismatch is already here, in modules: well over 200 GW of nameplate capacity running at roughly 35–40% utilization. Cells are next. Capacity is expected to grow from about 35 GW to as much as 100 GW within a year, turning today’s shortage into a surplus faster than many expect. Wafers could follow around 2028–29 if every announced project is built. Polysilicon is the exception: too little supply, not too much.
Margins move to the scarce link. Today that is cells. As cell capacity arrives, that premium will narrow and margin will shift upstream to wafers for a period, even while modules stay oversupplied.
Could ALMM List-III increase domestic wafer prices? How much of a premium over imports can manufacturers absorb before project economics are affected?
In the first year or two, yes. Early supply will be concentrated, plants will still be ramping yields, and much of the first capacity belongs to integrated groups that will use it themselves.
But perspective matters. At today’s prices, wafers are well under a tenth of the price of a domestic-content module, so even a 20–25% wafer premium adds only 2-3% at module level. The real risk is stacking, where premiums on wafers, cells and modules compound into project tariffs. What the market can absorb depends on discipline across the whole chain.
Will the requirement for three independent manufacturers with a combined 15 GW capacity under ALMM List-III adequately address supply concentration concerns?
The threshold is a sensible safeguard. The initial List-III will not be issued until at least three independent units with a combined 15 GW are available, so the mandate cannot bite on a single-supplier market.
But eligibility is not availability. With cells, most listed capacity is captive and only a small fraction reaches the open market. Wafers could follow the same pattern, so merchant availability is the number to watch in the first year.
Which operating metrics will determine whether Indian ingot and wafer manufacturing can compete globally without regulatory protection?
Three numbers. First, silicon consumption per saleable watt. It captures yield, kerf loss and wafer thickness together, and since polysilicon is the largest cost item, this is where competitiveness is won or lost. Second, puller productivity: kilograms per puller per day, and how many ingots each crucible delivers. Third, energy cost per kilogram, combining consumption and tariff.
The honest test is simple: could the plant sell profitably at import parity if List-III disappeared tomorrow? If not, the regulation is carrying the business.
What must India do to become a competitive solar wafer exporter, and where could its first major export opportunities emerge?
Capacity is necessary but not sufficient. We need non-Chinese polysilicon because traceability is what export customers will pay for. We need quality proven over years, because cell makers qualify wafer suppliers slowly. And we need power and financing costs closer to global benchmarks.
On price alone, Indian wafers will not undercut Chinese wafers for some years. But markets are no longer purely open. The United States is adding cell capacity far faster than wafer capacity, and the new duties on Indian cells and modules make wafers the more credible export product. The first customers will be overseas cell makers seeking a qualified second source with traceable supply.

global-economics-38200fc22f.headline: SEBI orders Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy to refund ₹546 crore; imposes ₹11.5 crore penalty
global-economics-38200fc22f.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-38200fc22f.fulltext:
Markets regulator SEBI on Friday directed Avadhut Sathe Trading Academy Pvt Ltd (ASTAPL) and its Founder Avadhut Sathe to refund Rs 546.17 crore collected from participants for providing unregistered investment advisory and research analyst services, along with interest of Rs 67.87 crore.
SEBI bars academy and founder from securities market
The regulator has also barred the academy and Sathe from accessing the securities market for two years or until compliance with the refund direction, whichever is later.
In its 171-page final order, the regulator imposed a total penalty of Rs 11.5 crore on the academy, Sathe and Gouri Avadhut Sathe for violations of securities market regulations.
The academy has been fined Rs 6 crore, Sathe has been fined Rs 4 crore, while Gouri Avadhut Sathe has been penalised Rs 1.5 crore.
Unregistered investment advice and misleading return claims
The regulator found that the academy and Sathe provided investment advice and research recommendations through paid programmes, sessions and WhatsApp groups without obtaining the required registration.
It also found that misleading promotional representations about returns were used to attract participants and that investment advice was provided without assessing the suitability of recommendations for recipients.
The order said the academy and Sathe had collected around Rs 601.38 crore from course participants since inception. However, based on the evidence examined, fees of Rs 546.17 crore attributable to the relevant programmes were identified for disgorgement and refund.
Five-month deadline for refunds
SEBI has directed the academy and Sathe to complete the refunds within five months of receiving the order. They have also been asked to publish notices in newspapers within 30 days, explaining the procedure for investors to claim refunds.
The regulator has further directed that their bank accounts remain frozen for debits until the required amounts are deposited into the designated account and SEBI’s Investor Protection and Education Fund, as applicable.
Gouri Avadhut Sathe barred for six months
Gouri Avadhut Sathe has been barred from accessing the securities market for six months. SEBI said her liability arose from a failure to exercise oversight.

India voter-roll protests widen as farmers set to join in
 By Bloomberg
Indian farmers who helped force Prime Minister Narendra Modi into a rare policy retreat four years ago are set to join nationwide protests against a contentious overhaul of voter rolls on Friday, widening a movement challenging the country’s Election Commission.
The Samyukt Kisan Morcha, a coalition of farmers’ organizations, is planning to march to the poll body’s headquarters in New Delhi from a nearby Sikh temple, according to P. Krishnaprasad, a member of SKM’s coordination committee. He expects police to block the march.
Farmers and trade unions are also expected to hold demonstrations in other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Their entry broadens a movement that has so far drawn much of its momentum from students, young people and opposition parties. The Samyukt Kisan Morcha had spearheaded the year-long agitation that pushed Modi to repeal contentious farm laws in 2021.
Security was noticeably lighter on Friday than during last week’s student-led protests, when authorities sealed off parts of central New Delhi with barricades and deployed riot police and paramilitary forces around government buildings and protest sites.

Krishnaprasad said organizers haven’t sought police permission for Friday’s demonstrations, saying peaceful protest is a constitutional right.
“Wherever the police stop us, we will stand there, we will keep our demands there, we will make the announcement, we will sing our national anthem and then we will disperse,” he said.
New Delhi has been hit by repeated protests over the election controversy in recent weeks. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi was detained by police earlier this month as part of demonstrations against the poll body, while the arrests of student leaders Saurav Das and Ranka, who were later released, added to tensions.

The furor was stoked by an Indian Express investigation last month that found Kumar’s two fellow commissioners repeatedly objected to aspects of a sweeping update of India’s electoral rolls that removed millions from draft voter lists. The poll body has denied any wrongdoing.

health-tech-ad23c2fc28.headline: STAT+: AI drug firm Pathos raises $237 million, pushing valuation to $3 billion
health-tech-ad23c2fc28.fulltext:
Pathos, an artificial intelligence-driven drug development company, announced on Friday it is raising $237 million in a Series E fundraising round led by Bristol Myers Squibb. The deal brings Pathos’ valuation to approximately $3 billion.
Pathos is also expanding from oncology to neurological conditions with new datasets from Tempus AI and a partnership with BMS that will first focus on Alzheimer’s treatments.
Most drugs that enter clinical trials never reach patients, but Pathos’ pitch is that AI can improve the odds. Its proprietary model, Foundry, operates thousands of agents that calculate the probability of success for its clinical assets. The agents analyze clinical data, genomics, biological specimen data, and competition from other developers. This information guides Pathos’s decision-making on which drugs to pursue, what populations to test them in, and how to design the clinical trials.
